div.p: Fixed priority schedulers are widely used for real-time systems, and there were efforts to improve the schedulability. For example, preemption threshold scheduling increases the schedulability by introducing non-preemptiveness during task execution. In this paper, we study another scheduling model that can improve the schedulability of tasks: quantum-based scheduling. When quantum-based scheduling is combined with priority-based scheduling, the quantum introduces a partially non-preemptive region which causes a priority inversion. We show that the nonpreemptiveness introduced by quantum-based scheduling can improve the schedulability of fixed priority tasks, and there is a task set which is not schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling but is schedulable by quantum-based scheduling. This paper also presents a method to calculate the worst case response time of tasks in quantum-based scheduling.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Although the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm is optimal for preemptive [16] and non-preemptive [11] realtime scheduling on a uniprocessor, fixed priority scheduling such as the Rate Monotonic (RM) algorithm [16] or the Deadline Monotonic (DM) method [3] was widely used in real-time systems because it is very easy to implement [5]. In general, preemptive schedulers give better schedulability than non-preemptive schedulers. However, it was shown that in the context of fixed priority scheduling, preemptive schedulers are not always superior to non-preemptive schedulers [7,17].

Preemption threshold scheduling [17] is a dual priority scheduling scheme that improves schedulability of fixed priority tasks. Introduction of a preemption threshold allows a task to disable preemption according to its preemption threshold, which may make the task schedulable, even though the task was not schedulable either by preemptive or non-preemptive schedulers. Further studies of preemption threshold scheduling can be found in [6,8,13], and the application of the preemption threshold to dynamic priority scheduling is discussed in [10].

In this paper, we analyze quantum-based scheduling of fixed priority periodic tasks to enhance the schedulability of tasks. Here is the definition of quantum-based scheduling from [1]: "Under quantum-based scheduling, processor time is allocated to tasks in discrete time units called quanta. When a processor is allocated to some task, that task is guaranteed to execute without preemption for q time units, where q is the length of the quantum, or until it terminates, whichever comes first." Thus, quantum-based scheduling is similar to preemption threshold scheduling in the sense that both provide a continuum of scheduling spaces: ". . . nonpreemptive and preemptive systems abstractly can be viewed as the extreme endpoints in a continuum of quantum-based systems: a nonpreemptive system results when q = ∞ and a fully preemptive system results when q = 0."

Quantum-based scheduling was applied to dynamic priority scheduling for efficient object sharing [1], flow protection in communication [15], and reduction of the scheduling overhead [4]. For fixed priority scheduling, [12] analyzed the disadvantages of the quantum for schedulability: a blocking time introduced by the non-preemptive region, due to quantum-based scheduling. [9] studied both threshold preemption and quantum-based scheduling (called delayed preemption in their work), and reported an empirical results that show quantum-based scheduling can increase processor utilization with RM priority assignment. The works in [4,9] allow a different quantum size for each task. In this paper, we also study the advantages of the quantum for schedulability. We found that a task set that is not schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling may be schedulable with quantum-based fixed priority scheduling, by carefully choosing a quantum size.

div.head: System model and example
div.p: A periodic task is denoted by τ i , and a periodic task set is represented by the collection of periodic tasks, τ = {τ i }. Each τ i is a three-tuple (T i , D i , C i ) where T i is the period, D i is the relative deadline, and C i is the worst case execution time. In this paper, we assume that
div.formula: T i ≥ D i ≥ C i > 0.
div.p: A concrete task has a specified release time, or the time of the first invocation. The difficulty of scheduling tasks can be affected by the release time [11]. A periodic task set is defined as schedulable if and only if all concrete task sets that can be generated from the periodic task set are schedulable. We consider only periodic task sets in this paper. For a given task τ i , we define hp(τ i ) as a subset of τ , which consists of tasks with priority higher than or equal to τ i (except τ i ). On the other hand, lp(τ i ) is the set of tasks with lower priority than τ i . Tasks are all independent and cannot be suspended by themselves.

Time is represented by an integer. Therefore time is discrete and clock ticks are indexed by integers, as in [11]. A quantum is a system variable, which is a unit of nonpreemptive execution. Because clock ticks are integerindexed, the quantum must also be an integer. When a task is scheduled, the task is assigned to the quantum and can execute during the quantum without being preempted by other tasks, unless it finishes its execution before the quantum expires. If the task finishes before the quantum expires, another task can be selected and starts its quantum.

Consider an example task set from [17]. There are three tasks τ 1 = (70, 50, 20), τ 2 = (80, 80, 20), and τ 3 = (200, 100, 35). As shown in [17], these tasks are not schedulable by preemptive or non-preemptive scheduling, but are schedulable with preemption threshold scheduling. We modify the example by increasing the worst case execution time of τ 1 to 25. Then the task set is not schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling as shown in Table 1.

By choosing an appropriate quantum size, we can make the modified tasks schedulable. In this case, there are many possible values of the quantum size. As an example we choose 20 as the quantum size. Figure 1 shows the worst case response time of τ 3 in RM priority ordering when the quantum size is 20.

Tasks are given their priority by RM priority assignment. In RM priority ordering, priority is higher for shorter period. In this example, τ 1 has the highest priority, τ 2 has the next, and τ 3 has the lowest. The higher priority tasks τ 1 and τ 2 are simultaneously released with τ 3 , which starts the critical instant of τ 3 . At time 25, the time quantum has not yet expired, but since τ 1 has finished its job, τ 2 is scheduled. At time 65, τ 3 exceeds the bounds of its quantum, but since there is no other task to execute, τ 3 is allowed to continue its execution. Though τ 1 is released again at time 70, since the time quantum of τ 3 has not yet expired, τ 3 completes its execution, to time 80. With the quantum size of 20, the worst case response times of tasks are: 44, 64, and 80 for τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 respectively.

div.head: The worst case response time under quantum-based scheduling
div.p: In our model, if the quantum size q = 1, quantumbased scheduling is equivalent to the fully preemptive scheduling since time is discrete. On the other hand, if q ≥ max 1≤i≤n {C i }, scheduling is equivalent to nonpreemptive scheduling. When 1 < q < max 1≤i≤n {C i }, the schedule can be considered as a mixture of preemptive scheduling and non-preemptive scheduling. But, since a task is non-preemptive during a maximum of q time units, quantum-based scheduling has some characteristics of nonpreemptive scheduling.

To obtain the worst case response time of a task in quantum-based scheduling, we can use previous results for non-preemptive scheduling. It is shown in [7] that the concept of level-i busy period is useful for non-preemptive scheduling. Level-i busy period is defined as a processor busy period in which only instances of tasks in hp(τ i ) and τ i execute [14].

div.head: Lemma 1
div.p: The worst case response time of a task τ i in nonpreemptive fixed priority scheduling is found in a level-i busy period obtained by simultaneously releasing τ i with all tasks in hp(τ i ) at time 0 and the task which has the longest execution time in lp(τ i ) at time -1.
From Lemma 1, we can see that a task in quantum-based fixed priority scheduling has the worst case response time during the same interval as shown in Theorem 1.

By Theorem 1, it follows that the maximum blocking time is bounded by the quantum size.
Lemma 2 When the quantum size is q, the maximum blocking time due to lower priority tasks is less than or equal to q -1.

Proof: By Theorem 1, a lower priority task can block a higher priority task only when it is released prior to the higher priority task. And the maximum blocking occurs when a lower priority task is released at time -1 while higher priority tasks are released at time 0. Thus the maximum blocking time cannot be greater than q -1 since the lower priority task can run non-preemptively only for q time units.

div.head: Comparison with preemption threshold scheduling
div.p: The basic idea of quantum-based scheduling is similar to the preemption threshold scheduling. Both scheduling schemes introduce priority inversion to enhance the processor utilization, and may reduce the number of preemptions hence context switching costs. But two scheduling schemes have some dissimilarities also.

Firstly, while the blocking time for a task τ i is bounded by the quantum size in quantum-based scheduling, it is max{C j |γ j ≥ π i > π j } in preemption threshold scheduling where γ j is the preemption threshold of τ j , π i is the priority of τ i , and π j is the priority of τ j . Thus when the worst case execution times of lower priority tasks are larger than higher priority tasks, it is possible that quantumbased scheduling have smaller blocking time than preemption threshold scheduling. And if we allow each task to have its own quantum size assigned as in [4] and [9], we can expect that blocking time in quantum-based scheduling will be smaller than preemption threshold scheduling.

Secondly, quantum-based scheduling guarantees at least q time units of non-preemptive region, while the nonpreemptive region in preemption threshold scheduling is determined in run time. Using the non-preemptiveness in quantum-based scheduling, we can use it to partially eliminate the need for locking operations by restricting the length of any critical section shorter than q, as pointed out in [9].

Thirdly, quantum-based scheduling can be used to implement real-time applications on general-purpose computers. Many conventional general-purpose operating systems such as Solaris and Windows XP provide quantum-based scheduling and priority-based scheduling. By comining the priority and the quantum, we can provide quantum-based fixed priority scheduling described in this paper. On the other hand, preemption threshold scheduling can optimize stack space utilization [8], thus it is useful in designing embedded systems that often have a limit on the amount of memory.

div.head: Conclusion and future work
div.p: We present some results of analysis of quantum-based fixed priority scheduling. Quantum-based scheduling is similar to preemption threshold scheduling, in the sense that it has advantages of both preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling: increased schedulability and reduced context switching. It was shown that for some tasks quantum-based scheduling can make tasks schedulable, even though the tasks are not schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling.

We present the calculation method for determining the worst case response time under quantum-based scheduling when priorities and the quantum size are pre-determined. The method has the same complexity as the worst case response time calculation under non-preemptive scheduling. Finding a feasible priority assignment for quantum-based scheduling can be done using the optimal priority assignment algorithm in [2,7].

The scheduling overhead of quantum-based scheduling in practice should be analyzed with empirical studies. From a practical perspective, preemption threshold scheduling offers many benefits other than an increase in schedulability: reduction of run-time overhead, reduction of memory usage, etc. Study on the characterisitcs of quantum-based scheduling to determine the practical benefits of quantumbased scheduling will be our future work.
